content.comment_body: I'm planning a roll-down shutter control system for 16 shutters. My setup will include: one [product_name] panel as the operator interface, one [product_name] module acting as the master with manual UP/DOWN button control, and eight [product_name] modules, each managing two shutters, all networked via Ethernet. According to the manual, up to 16 network connections are supported in the [product_name] network, which suits my design of 10 connections. However, I need to send a total of 32 UP/DOWN commands, and have noticed the manual states only 8 static connections are available. Is this setup feasible for my requirements? I would appreciate feedback since I am not experienced with the latest [product_name] series. Thanks.
I'm not sure I fully understand, but one [product_name] can communicate with 8 other [product_name] modules. You can assign several network inputs or outputs to a single connection.
A [product_name] can handle up to 16 connections: 8 static and 8 dynamic. This means it can connect with up to 16 other [product_name] modules.

If you transmit bytes or words instead of individual UP/DOWN commands, only one connection per [product_name] module is needed. Use 1 or 0 to represent UP/DOWN, assigning each shutter a specific bit within a 32-bit word. Each module then extracts the relevant bits to control its assigned shutters. If you need a neutral state (neither up nor down), use an additional 32 bits to enable the commands, combining this with the UP/DOWN commands through logic operations. For instance, the first byte could be split: one part for enable, one part for shutter commands, allowing you to signal which shutter is enabled and the direction command. The logic for each module can then be built accordingly, though this is for simplicity rather than efficiency.
Thanks to everyone, things are much clearer now.
Combine 8 connections into one [product_name] and consolidate the data before sending it to your master [product_name].

analysis.insight_summary: Participants discussed implementing a distributed shutter control system using multiple interconnected automation modules over Ethernet. Key insights focused on navigating limitations in static network connections and strategies for efficiently encoding control signals. Initial uncertainties about connection counts and data handling were addressed collaboratively, leading to improved understanding of system capabilities and configuration recommendations.
analysis.user_expectations: The user expects to efficiently send all required control commands within network and connection constraints mentioned in the documentation. They are looking for advice on structuring module communication to ensure reliable shutter operation and clarity about the optimal technical approach.
